Reporter Seth Kantor says he spoke briefly with Ruby at Parkland; Wilma Tice also says she saw Ruby there. (Ruby denied it; the Warren Commission doubted Kantor, the HSCA thought him probably right.)
Reporter Harry McCormick brings Sorrels to Zapruder, who agrees to give the Secret Service a copy if it isn't given to the media.
A second search of the Depository begins after 1:30; employees are told not to discuss the case, even with family.

ATF agent Frank Ellsworth, in that search, told the Secret Service a detective found the rifle on the fourth or fifth floor, not with the shells, which with the "Mauser" description suggests to the La Fontaines a second gun. Kilduff announces the President's death; it goes out on the wires.
Time's Hugh Sidey recalls Kilduff reading that the President died at about 1 p.m., then weeping in a side office: "Oh, that man's head."
Ruth Paine tells Marina, hanging laundry in Irving, that Kennedy is dead and the shots reportedly came from the building where Lee works; Marina doesn't respond.

Johnson boards Air Force One, tells the pilot it won't leave without the President's body, and has the shades drawn and TV on. He tells O'Donnell that Robert Kennedy advised swearing in there and that Judge Sarah Hughes is coming.

Agents secure the plane. Youngblood says he'll stick to Johnson like glue; Johnson calls for Judge Hughes. FBI agent Vincent Drain says seats were removed for the casket, which had to be tilted up to get it aboard. (The chronology repeats that the Tippit gunman hid behind a Texaco station as police converged.)
Police are drawn to the Jefferson branch library by a report that the suspect is inside; some researchers think it was a diversion. Oswald is near the Texas Theatre about this time.
Police at the library report "wrong man." The chronology asks how they knew without knowing the right man, and notes the library was a block from Ruby's apartment and frequented by Oswald.
Myers says an officer mistook Adrian Hamby, running into the library, for the suspect.
FBI headquarters' Alan Belmont orders all offices to locate bombing suspects, Klan members and other extremists.

(Robert Kennedy's "one of your guys did it" to Haynes Johnson.) The book Farewell America claims Secret Service chief Rowley soon told Robert Kennedy there were three or four gunmen, and that Behn told Sorrels "It's a plot." Myers asks why Oswald risked returning to busy Jefferson Boulevard unless the theater was his destination.

A man slips into the Texas Theatre without paying. Burroughs says it couldn't have been Oswald, who'd been inside since shortly after 1:00, which would clear him of Tippit's murder. Shoe-store manager Johnny Brewer, who saw a man duck from passing police cars, tells cashier Julia Postal; only on December 6 does he mention a brown shirt. Postal didn't think she sold him a ticket and sold 24 that day.

A tip leads police to a car seen on Commerce Street; its driver, picked up in Fort Worth, says he came from Ranger to visit a friend and stayed for the parade, and is released when Oswald's arrest is announced.
Channel 2 reports the Depository is being secured, an hour and five minutes after the shots.
An officer at the Tippit scene radios an eyewitness description of the gunman, armed with a .32 dark automatic; Sgt. Hill soon says the shells indicate an automatic .38 rather than a pistol.
Tippit's autopsy report isn't in the Warren Commission volumes.
Captain W.R. Westbrook sends squads to search west of the Tippit scene.
Undertaker Vernon O'Neal brings a 400-pound bronze casket to Parkland. In Tampa, lawyer Frank Ragano says Hoffa called gloating that Bobby would now be out as attorney general.
A Hoover memo records calling Robert Kennedy with the first flash and being told to do whatever the FBI could.

In the theater, the pregnant woman who sat by Oswald goes up to the balcony and is never seen again. Westbrook and FBI agent Barrett come in the back, perhaps looking for the name in the Tippit-scene wallet.
Brewer checks the concession stand, balcony and exits with Burroughs, then has Postal call the police; she says the man ducks every time a siren goes by.

Police cars race to the theater on a report the suspect is in the balcony. Officers who enter from the front go up; Walker, McDonald and Hutson come in the back, where Hutson counts seven patrons on the main floor, including Oswald, Jack Davis, John Gibson and George Applin.
Applin told the Commission a man at the back watched the arrest calmly; in 1979 he said he later recognized him as Ruby and had been afraid to say so (Crossfire).

The chronology wonders why so many police answered a ticket-skipping call, citing Matthew Smith's story of police already waiting in an alley. A Secret Service veteran later claimed "we lost a man that day," echoing the false early reports.

Ruby arrives at the Carousel and closes the club for the night, makes calls and watches TV. Zapruder, his partner, Sorrels and McCormick go to the Morning News, then WFAA, where Zapruder is interviewed live.
Senior engineer Darrell Tomlinson finds a nearly pristine bullet on a Parkland stretcher; it becomes CE 399.

Hoover told Johnson within a week the bullet came from the President's stretcher, which would rule it out as the single bullet. Fragments found under Mrs. Connally's seat have since disappeared, and an agent finds another skull piece on the flight home. Dr. Shaw tells reporters a bullet remains in Connally's thigh. In the Senate, Don Reynolds's testimony about a $100,000 TFX payoff to Johnson via Bobby Baker (denied by Baker) is cut off by the news.
Radio Free Europe broadcasts the news to Eastern Europe.
Lt. Day leaves the Depository carrying the rifle.
Inspector Sawyer asks detectives to pick up Charles Givens, a Black porter with a police record who left the building.

Brewer opens the stage door to find police with guns drawn and leads them in. Officer Nick McDonald orders Oswald up; Oswald draws his pistol and they struggle until he is subdued (one witness said he was pistol-whipped). Officers had first questioned an unidentified young man in the balcony whom a "manager" said had been there since noon, though no manager was on duty; police reports even say Oswald was arrested in the balcony. Of 24 patrons, police recorded only two names.

Nixon cancels his afternoon and stays in watching the coverage; told jokingly that better makeup might have made him president, he says he'd be dead too. Police were looking for a man in a white shirt and jacket in the balcony but focus on a man in a brown shirt on the main floor. Officers hear the snap of the revolver misfiring; the FBI later notes a dented primer and bent firing pin. Westbrook orders him out fast, and Postal hears an officer say they have their man on both counts, calling him Oswald.
Walt Brown notes the search for other evidence or assassins stopped once Oswald became the suspect.
No report shows anyone checked his ID before an officer named him "Oswald" to Postal; WFAA film shows police looking through the wallet from the Tippit scene.
FBI agent Bardwell Odum and others describe a brown jacket; Oswald actually wore a brown shirt over a white T-shirt.

Oswald tells Fritz he changed his trousers at the rooming house, and the next day says shirt too, describing a reddish button-down shirt and gray trousers in his dresser; police inventory a brown button-down shirt and gray trousers there.
Those gray trousers match what Bledsoe, Jones and Whaley described. Police at the Depository find an unclaimed blue "Sir Jac" jacket.

Marina said Oswald had two jackets, blue and gray; she identified the blue one from the Depository and the gray one (CE 162) from the parking lot. Meagher doubts Westbrook found it, and police never showed it to Oswald.
Oswald complained he wasn't allowed a jacket for a lineup like the others; the chronology asks why police didn't put him in the gray jacket before witnesses.
CE 162 is a light gray zipper jacket; Benavides recalled light beige.
Markham: a short grayish-tan jacket, open in front; she didn't recognize CE 162.
Scoggins gave no independent description; Barbara Davis said a dark coat.
William Arthur Smith: a sport coat of some kind; Virginia Davis: light brown tan jacket.
Ted Callaway: a light tannish-gray windbreaker, same type but more tan. Earlene Roberts couldn't identify it.
Frazier couldn't recognize the gray jacket.
Only Sam Guinyard described and identified it without qualification.
The chronology tallies the rest as failing to describe or identify it, and notes the same witnesses didn't recognize the brown shirt.

In the car Oswald is calm and quiet, protesting he only carried a pistol in a movie; told he killed a policeman, he remarks you can only fry for that. Hill says he found six rounds in the revolver; five more were in Oswald's pocket. The chronology notes no box of either brand was found among his things.

Hill says Detective Bentley found a Selective Service card for "Alek J. Hidell" in his wallet, but none of the arresting officers' early December reports mention it, and early publicity was about "O.H. Lee," not Hidell. Marina first denied the alias, then said he used it; she said she signed "Hidell" on his FPCC card. Bernard Haire, behind the theater, saw a flushed young man brought out the back and put in a police car, and learned 25 years later that Oswald was taken out the front.
Captain Talbert and officers question a boy in the alley near an idling pickup; Talbert was among the few who filed no arrest report and wasn't asked about it by the Commission.
Offered a chance to hide his face, Oswald says he has nothing to be ashamed of.

The Warren Report describes reporters and cameramen crowding Oswald from the basement elevator to the homicide office, and his walking the 20-foot corridor past them at least 15 times over the weekend, cameras and microphones in his face.

Oswald is brought to Fritz's third-floor office. Meagher notes no question in his interrogations suggests the police or FBI suspected a conspiracy, and Tippit's name doesn't appear in the early questions.
Between 1:00 and 2:00, agent Richard Johnsen takes the stretcher bullet from O.P. Wright; Tomlinson later says it looked different from CE 399.

FBI examiner Robert Frazier testified the bullet was clean, without blood, tissue or fibers; Cyril Wecht calls that nearly impossible for a bullet that passed through clothing and two men. The FBI's spectrographic results were never put in evidence.

In 1993 Parkland's former nursing director Elizabeth Wright told researcher Wallace Milam her husband, security chief O.P. Wright, also found an unfired .38 Special on a gurney that day, which she had kept.
The Warren Commission ruled out the President's stretcher as the source, saying he stayed on it until placed in the casket and it was then moved to Trauma Room 2.
In 1964 none of the men in the chain of possession (Tomlinson, Wright, Johnsen, Rowley) could positively identify CE 399 as the bullet found.
The bronze casket is wheeled out to O'Neal's hearse.
The chronology claims the casket came back to O'Neal with green paint marks instead of blood, and that oxygen tanks and a body bag taken with it suggest a substitution; photos show the handles down.

From Air Force One Johnson calls Robert Kennedy, Abe Fortas (asking about Reynolds's testimony) and Dallas lawyer Waddy Bullion about his stocks. Marshals guard Hickory Hill. O'Donnell is overheard saying they'll take it back in '68. Robert Kennedy sends Jack Miller of the Criminal Division to Dallas.

Film by the Dallas Cinema Associates shows a different rifle, short-stocked and heavy-barreled, perhaps an Enfield, brought down the Depository fire escape; officials said in 1967 it was a security man's. (Weatherford's rooftop rifle is mentioned again.)

The chronology says one photo of Day dusting the rifle shows no clip while another of him carrying it shows one, and that the sling swivels appear on the side rather than the bottom as in the backyard photo.

It cites Life photos as showing the rifle is a rare Mussolini-bodyguard variant. The FBI quickly took interest in a Johnson semiautomatic .30-06 tied to anti-Castro raiders Hemming and Loran Hall, which Hall and a Hispanic man reclaimed from a California detective's office a week before the assassination.
Detective Richard Hathcock told the HSCA that Hemming and Hall pawned the rifle with him; Garrison later showed him a photo of a rifle found in Dealey Plaza that looked just like it.
FBI agent Jerry Crow questioned Hathcock and his associate Roy Payne the next day; Payne described the rifle as accurate and reclaimed 10–15 days before the assassination.

Payne said Hall told him on November 18 he was flying to Dallas, and later that he was in the Dallas Hilton lobby during the shooting (Hall told Dick Russell he was in California). Hemming claimed Hall stole rifles from him and gave a long account of Hathcock and a mob-money story.

Mechanic T.F. White sees a man in a red 1961 Falcon idling in the El Chico lot five blocks from the theater, who speeds off when approached; White later says he looked like Oswald and wore a white T-shirt.

Told Oswald was already in jail, White still says the man was possibly identical. The plate he noted belonged to a 1957 Plymouth owned by Carl Mather of Collins Radio, a friend of Tippit, who was nervous when reporters asked and talked to the HSCA only with immunity.
An FBI report confirms plate PP4537 was Mather's. The HSCA dismissed the incident; James Douglass calls the odds against coincidence astronomical.

The chronology notes Oswald once visited Collins executive Admiral Henry Bruton with de Mohrenschildt, Collins's Southeast Asia radio contract, and a boat leased to Collins, the Rex, captured by Cuba in November and said by an exile aboard to be running CIA arms.
Castro said the arms were for assassinating Cuban leaders.
Its scenario: an Oswald double in a car traced to Tippit's friend at a CIA-linked firm.
Brading is still held at the sheriff's office; his companion Morgan Brown checks out of the Cabana abruptly.
Sorrels asks Zapruder for copies; Zapruder had refused police who came brandishing shotguns and insisted on a federal representative.
The limousine leaves Parkland, driven by agent George Hickey with a police officer, and is flown to Washington on a C-130.
The New York Stock Exchange closes early after a 24-point drop; the chronology claims short sellers made huge profits.
A Hoover memo: Shanklin reports the President in very poor condition but alive, shots from a fourth floor with a Winchester; asks if Robert Kennedy is coming.

After a heated argument, the Secret Service removes the body over Dallas medical examiner Earl Rose's objection that Texas law requires a local autopsy and the chain of evidence will be broken; Kellerman says they'll take care of it in Washington.
A policeman at Rose's side says they can't go; O'Brien, O'Donnell and Burkley push through. Judge Ward hears DA Wade say he has no objection. The casket is wheeled out.
Agent Andy Berger drives the ambulance to Love Field; Kellerman and O'Donnell radio ahead to let it through and have the pilot ready.

Sorrels told the FBI he stayed at Parkland until the body left, but photos show him back at Dealey Plaza, where he finds two witnesses to shots from the "Oswald window," learns Oswald is the missing employee, and takes Zapruder to Kodak.
